summary:
Same-sex marriage is not licensed in American Samoa. The territory's Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing in July 2015 whether the United States Supreme Court's marriage-equality ruling applied, and the Governor stated at the time that it did not, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application for a marriage licence then, and none has applied to date.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements, and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. The article sets out the litigation route: the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Reporting from the territory in July 2024 described the local ban as still treated as operative on the island and its durability under the Fourteenth Amendment as an open question, with a survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor testing the issue.

Under the Respect for Marriage Act signed on 13 December 2022, American Samoa must recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. American Samoa remains the only part of the United States, alongside certain Native American tribal jurisdictions, that does not licence same-sex marriage.

The territory's judiciary has operated on the premise that the 2015 ruling does not automatically apply. In January 2016, at his confirmation hearing for District Court judge, Fiti Alexander Sunia told Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean that he had not read the Supreme Court decision, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

In March 2003 the Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed. The bill had been introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster to preempt marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who oppose such marriages on Christian grounds.

Birth certificates in American Samoa are altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, under a High Court ruling that the Office of Vital Statistics applies to applications from transgender individuals. The office changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Protection machinery has been used locally. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, following a June 2023 federal civil action that cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

American Samoan society is highly religious, and conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality tend to dominate. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. Against that, fa'afafine, boys raised as girls to take an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, are described in the sources as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the territory is described as tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, and frames contemporary activity as a reclaiming of Pacific gender identities after colonial suppression. SOFIAS annually organises events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are popular, with families generally turning out in support of candidates.

A 2009 travel column reported that homosexuality is widely accepted in Samoan culture, while reserved behaviour by people of all orientations is expected under the fa'amatai chiefly system; it described Western gay men being courted by fa'afafine transgender locals. Local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands the homeland of fa'afafine culture.
tangentialFactors:
In July 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory unsure whether the federal marriage-equality ruling applied, while Puerto Rico, the United States Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it; the territory's Attorney General said applicability was still being reviewed.

The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to the age of "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and as "daughter," a drafting feature that bears on how a marriage application would be processed.

The territory's criminal law does not punish consensual sodomy: the 1979 revision, effective 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and persons unable to consent, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, criminalised male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian sex.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, runs annual events and festivals and campaigns for the fa'afafine community; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, and fa'afafine beauty pageants draw family support.

Residents live under a highly religious, conservative social code in which reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations and open displays of affection may offend, alongside a cultural tradition of raising some boys as girls to serve an important domestic role in communal life.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 federal marriage-equality ruling is legally operative in American Samoa remains unresolved: the territory's officials treated it as inapplicable in 2015 and a District Court judge in 2016 acted on that premise, a 2026 law review article by local practitioners concludes it does apply, and reporting from July 2024 described the ban as still treated as operative on-island with its constitutional durability an open question. No same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence, so no court has ruled.

Current United States passport and identity-document policy for transgender and non-binary travellers is not sourced to American Samoa-specific material in this inventory; the sources cited are national reporting and advocacy guidance, and the territory's own document practice is covered only for birth certificates.
